questions.stem: This midsagittal diagram of the head and neck labels the epiglottis at the entrance to the larynx. What is its primary function?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Covering the laryngeal opening during swallowing

explanation.summary: During swallowing the epiglottis folds back over the laryngeal inlet, directing food into the esophagus and protecting the airway from aspiration.
explanation.whyCorrect: During swallowing the epiglottis folds back over the laryngeal inlet, directing food into the esophagus and protecting the airway from aspiration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Voice is produced by vibration of the vocal folds in the glottis, not by the epiglottis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Warming and humidifying air is done mainly by the nasal conchae and mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dust is filtered by nasal hairs, turbinates, and the mucociliary escalator, not the epiglottis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucus in the nasopharynx comes from goblet cells and submucosal glands of the respiratory mucosa.

questions.stem: This airway wall shows a mucosa of tall pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, a submucosa, and an underlying plate of pale hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae. Which structure is this section most consistent with?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium resting on a mucosa/submucosa supported by hyaline cartilage is characteristic of the trachea and large bronchi of the conducting airways.

questions.stem: A small airway with folded epithelium is encircled by a layer of smooth muscle and surrounded by thin-walled air spaces (alveoli), with no cartilage present. What airway is shown?

explanation.summary: A small conducting airway lacking cartilage and glands but wrapped by a relatively prominent smooth muscle layer, surrounded by alveoli, identifies a bronchiole; the absence of cartilage distinguishes it from bronchi.
explanation.whyCorrect: A small conducting airway lacking cartilage and glands but wrapped by a relatively prominent smooth muscle layer, surrounded by alveoli, identifies a bronchiole; the absence of cartilage distinguishes it from bronchi.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A segmental bronchus has cartilage plates and submucosal glands in its wall, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An alveolar sac is a cluster of alveoli without its own epithelium-lined lumen wrapped by smooth muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The trachea has C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings and pseudostratified ciliated epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A pulmonary artery has an endothelial lining with an elastic and muscular media, not folded airway epithelium.

questions.stem: This lung section (40X) shows a large conducting airway lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. What is the primary function of this epithelial lining?

explanation.summary: The bronchial epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells; cilia sweep mucus-trapped debris up toward the pharynx (mucociliary escalator). Gas exchange occurs only in alveoli, not conducting airways.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bronchial epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells; cilia sweep mucus-trapped debris up toward the pharynx (mucociliary escalator). Gas exchange occurs only in alveoli, not conducting airways.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sound is generated by the vocal folds in the larynx, not by bronchial epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Odorants are detected by olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surfactant is secreted by type II pneumocytes in the alveoli, not by conducting airway epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gas exchange occurs only across the thin alveolar wall, not through thick conducting airway epithelium.

choices.label: E

explanation.whyCorrect: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs, and alveoli make up the respiratory zone where gas exchange occurs, distinguishing it from the purely conducting airways.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The conducting zone ends at the terminal bronchioles and does not include structures with alveoli.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The pleural cavity is the space between visceral and parietal pleura, outside the lung parenchyma.

questions.stem: In this diagram of an alveolus, what is the principal function of the Type 2 pneumocyte?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Forming the thin barrier for gas diffusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conducting air toward the alveolar duct

explanation.whyCorrect: Type 2 pneumocytes (cuboidal cells) secrete surfactant, which reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse. Type 1 pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface, and dust cells (macrophages) clear debris.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mucus is produced by goblet cells and submucosal glands in conducting airways, not alveoli.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The thin diffusion barrier is formed by flat type I pneumocytes, not the cuboidal type II cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phagocytosis of dust is done by alveolar macrophages (dust cells).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumocytes line alveoli and do not conduct air; conduction is the role of the airway tree.

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: At the edge of this lung section a thin fibrous membrane (bracketed) covers the alveolar tissue. What is the functional role of this membrane?

explanation.summary: The visceral pleura is a serous membrane covering the lung; together with the parietal pleura and pleural fluid it minimizes friction as the lung expands and recoils during breathing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The visceral pleura is a serous membrane covering the lung; together with the parietal pleura and pleural fluid it minimizes friction as the lung expands and recoils during breathing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Surfactant is secreted by type II pneumocytes inside alveoli, not by the pleura.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gas exchange happens across alveolar walls, not across the pleural surface.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Air is conducted by bronchi and bronchioles; the pleura is a serous covering of the lung.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucus is produced by goblet cells and glands in conducting airways, not the pleural mesothelium.

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This high-power view shows the epithelium that lines the trachea, with an apical row of cilia and a basal lamina propria. What is its main functional role?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Moving a mucus layer with trapped particles

explanation.summary: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines the trachea; coordinated ciliary beating propels mucus and trapped debris upward (mucociliary escalator).
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines the trachea; coordinated ciliary beating propels mucus and trapped debris upward (mucociliary escalator).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Airway epithelium is not specialized for nutrient absorption; that is the role of intestinal enterocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gas exchange occurs across the thin alveolar wall, not across tracheal epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although scattered neuroendocrine cells exist, hormone secretion is not the main role of this ciliated epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Filtration of plasma occurs in glomeruli, not across airway epithelium.

questions.stem: This specialized pseudostratified epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity contains bipolar sensory neurons (ON) among supporting (S) and basal (B) cells. What special sense does it mediate?

explanation.whyCorrect: The olfactory epithelium contains bipolar olfactory receptor neurons whose cilia detect odorants; supporting (sustentacular) and basal cells complete the epithelium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hearing is mediated by hair cells of the cochlea in the inner ear.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Taste is mediated by taste buds on the tongue and palate, not by bipolar neurons in the nasal roof.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vision is mediated by photoreceptors in the retina.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Balance is sensed by hair cells of the vestibular apparatus in the inner ear.

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram maps epithelial types onto the upper airway, showing stratified squamous epithelium in the oropharynx rather than ciliated epithelium. Why is stratified squamous epithelium found there?

choices.label: C
choices.text: To absorb nutrients from swallowed food

choices.label: D
choices.text: To improve ciliary clearance of particles

choices.label: E
choices.text: To maximize gas exchange with blood

explanation.summary: The oropharynx is a shared food and air passage; stratified squamous epithelium resists the abrasion of food boluses, unlike the delicate ciliated epithelium of purely respiratory passages.
explanation.whyCorrect: The oropharynx is a shared food and air passage; stratified squamous epithelium resists the abrasion of food boluses, unlike the delicate ciliated epithelium of purely respiratory passages.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Stratified squamous epithelium is not a mucus-secreting epithelium; goblet cells belong to respiratory epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pharynx does not absorb nutrients; absorption occurs in the small intestine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stratified squamous epithelium lacks cilia, so it cannot improve ciliary clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gas exchange happens only in alveoli; thick multilayered epithelium would impede diffusion.

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This respiratory epithelium contains ciliated columnar cells, basal cells, and goblet cells. What is the role of the goblet cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beating rhythmically to propel the mucus layer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secreting mucus that traps inhaled particles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carrying out gas exchange with capillaries

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serving as stem cells to regenerate the epithelium

explanation.summary: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps debris and microbes; the cilia of columnar cells then sweep this mucus toward the pharynx, while basal cells act as the regenerative reserve.
explanation.whyCorrect: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps debris and microbes; the cilia of columnar cells then sweep this mucus toward the pharynx, while basal cells act as the regenerative reserve.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Propulsion of the mucus layer is done by the ciliated columnar cells, not goblet cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gas exchange occurs in alveoli, not in conducting airway epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Basal cells serve as the stem cell reserve for regenerating the epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Odorant detection is performed by olfactory receptor neurons in the nasal roof.

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This nonkeratinizing stratified epithelium overlying a lamina propria lines a region shared by the digestive and respiratory tracts. Which region is it most likely from?

explanation.summary: Nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium lines areas subject to abrasion such as the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, protecting against the passage of food.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium lines areas subject to abrasion such as the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, protecting against the passage of food.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alveoli are lined by simple squamous type I and cuboidal type II pneumocytes, not stratified epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchi are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nasal roof is lined by olfactory epithelium, a pseudostratified epithelium with bipolar neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium and is purely respiratory.

questions.topicName: Histology of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram shows O2 and CO2 crossing the structure between alveolar air and blood. By what mechanism do these gases cross this barrier?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Secondary active transport coupled to sodium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osmosis of dissolved gas with water

explanation.summary: Gas exchange across the blood-air barrier is passive: O2 and CO2 diffuse down their respective partial pressure gradients through the thin Type 1 pneumocyte, fused basement membrane, and capillary endothelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gas exchange across the blood-air barrier is passive: O2 and CO2 diffuse down their respective partial pressure gradients through the thin Type 1 pneumocyte, fused basement membrane, and capillary endothelium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gases do not use sodium-coupled transporters; they are small and lipid-soluble enough to cross membranes directly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No ATP-driven pump moves O2 or CO2; the partial pressure gradient alone drives their movement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osmosis is the movement of water, not of dissolved gases, across membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Facilitated diffusion requires carrier proteins, which O2 and CO2 do not need to cross the barrier.

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This cross-section shows a thin-walled air sac with squamous lining cells, a scattered wandering phagocyte, a cuboidal cell secreting a thin film into the airspace, and a surrounding capillary containing red cells. Which cell type here is responsible for reducing surface tension and preventing collapse of this structure?

explanation.summary: The cuboidal type II pneumocyte secretes pulmonary surfactant, which lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration. Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface, and macrophages clear debris; endothelial cells line the capillary.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cuboidal type II pneumocyte secretes pulmonary surfactant, which lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration. Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface, and macrophages clear debris; endothelial cells line the capillary.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I pneumocytes are flat squamous cells forming the gas-exchange surface; they do not secrete surfactant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Capillary endothelial cells line the blood vessel and do not secrete into the airspace.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alveolar macrophages are the wandering phagocytes that clear debris, not secretors of surfactant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ciliated columnar cells line the conducting airways and are not present in the alveolar wall.

questions.stem: This H&E-stained section shows thin-walled air sacs opening off a larger conducting passage. From which organ is this tissue taken?

explanation.whyCorrect: The delicate polygonal air spaces (alveoli) with thin capillary-containing septa opening off a bronchiolar lumen are the defining histologic architecture of lung parenchyma, specialized for gas exchange.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Spleen shows red pulp sinusoids and white pulp lymphoid follicles, not air-filled spaces.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thyroid shows follicles filled with pink colloid, which contain protein rather than air.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Liver shows hepatocyte plates, sinusoids, and portal triads, not alveoli.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Kidney shows glomeruli and tubules, not thin-walled air sacs opening off an airway.

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In this magnified developing lung, the airway is still lined by tall cuboidal cells with only sparse nearby capillaries. Which stage of lung development does this represent?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Terminal air sac stage with surfactant

explanation.summary: A thick cuboidal epithelium separated from capillaries by abundant mesoderm indicates an immature stage with a thick air-blood barrier; the epithelium has not yet thinned into type 1 pneumocytes needed for efficient gas exchange.
explanation.whyCorrect: A thick cuboidal epithelium separated from capillaries by abundant mesoderm indicates an immature stage with a thick air-blood barrier; the epithelium has not yet thinned into type 1 pneumocytes needed for efficient gas exchange.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The saccular stage has thinned walls with type I pneumocytes and close capillary contact, unlike the tall cuboidal lining here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The adult lung has thin alveolar walls with type I pneumocytes in contact with dense capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The alveolar stage has mature alveoli with thin septa, not tall cuboidal epithelium with sparse capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Terminal sacs with surfactant production form later, when the epithelium has thinned and capillaries abut the airspaces.

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This magnified alveolar wall shows flat cells lining most of the surface and scattered rounded granular cells at the corners, adjacent to capillaries. What is the key function of the rounded granular cell type shown?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of the thin gas-diffusion surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conduction of air to the alveoli

explanation.summary: The cuboidal granular cells are type 2 pneumocytes, which secrete surfactant that lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse; the flat cells are type 1 pneumocytes forming the diffusion barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cuboidal granular cells are type 2 pneumocytes, which secrete surfactant that lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse; the flat cells are type 1 pneumocytes forming the diffusion barrier.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucus is produced by goblet cells and glands in conducting airways, not by alveolar cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The thin diffusion surface is formed by the flat type I cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phagocytosis is the role of alveolar macrophages, which are wandering cells rather than wall-lining cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Conduction of air is the role of the airway tree, not of cells within the alveolar wall.

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This timeline maps lung development onto gestational weeks. At approximately which point does the lung first become capable of supporting respiration (gas exchange)?

explanation.summary: Respiration becomes possible near the canalicular-to-saccular transition (~24-26 weeks) once a thin air-blood barrier forms and type 2 pneumocytes begin surfactant production, which is why this marks the threshold of viability for premature infants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Respiration becomes possible near the canalicular-to-saccular transition (~24-26 weeks) once a thin air-blood barrier forms and type 2 pneumocytes begin surfactant production, which is why this marks the threshold of viability for premature infants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: At 12 weeks the lung is in the pseudoglandular stage, with only branching ducts and no gas-exchange surface.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alveoli continue to multiply into childhood, but gas exchange becomes possible long before birth, not decades later.
whyWrongByChoice.D: At 6 weeks the lung bud is just branching in the embryonic period, with no respiratory tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Premature infants can breathe from about 24-26 weeks, so gas exchange is possible well before birth.

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This sequence shows the foregut giving rise to a ventral outgrowth that is progressively partitioned. What process is being illustrated?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of the diaphragm from the septum transversum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fusion of the pleural and pericardial cavities

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rotation of the primitive heart tube

choices.label: E
choices.text: Separation of the trachea from the esophagus

explanation.summary: The respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut and is separated from the future esophagus by tracheoesophageal ridges that fuse into a septum; failure of this process produces tracheoesophageal fistula.
explanation.whyCorrect: The respiratory diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut and is separated from the future esophagus by tracheoesophageal ridges that fuse into a septum; failure of this process produces tracheoesophageal fistula.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neural tube closure involves dorsal ectoderm folding, not a ventral foregut outgrowth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The septum transversum forms part of the diaphragm from mesoderm, not by partitioning a foregut outgrowth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pleural and pericardial cavities are separated by pleuropericardial membranes, not fused, and this is unrelated to the foregut.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heart tube looping involves the cardiac mesoderm, not a diverticulum of the foregut.

questions.topicName: Development of the Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: From 28 to 56 days, the paired outgrowths shown undergo repeated dichotomous division into progressively smaller branches. What does this branching establish?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conducting airway tree and lung lobes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pulmonary venous return to the left atrium

explanation.summary: Sequential division of secondary and tertiary bronchial buds during the pseudoglandular period lays down the branching conducting airways and defines the lobar pattern (three lobes on the right, two on the left).
explanation.whyCorrect: Sequential division of secondary and tertiary bronchial buds during the pseudoglandular period lays down the branching conducting airways and defines the lobar pattern (three lobes on the right, two on the left).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The pleural mesothelium derives from surrounding splanchnic mesoderm, not from branching of the bronchial buds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bronchial smooth muscle derives from surrounding mesoderm, and airways do not have true sphincters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary veins develop as an outgrowth of the left atrium, not from branching of bronchial buds.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The alveolar-capillary membrane forms much later, in the saccular and alveolar stages, not between 28 and 56 days.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram shows the great vessels of the neck. Why does the right common carotid artery arise differently from the left?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both arise directly from the ascending aorta before the arch

choices.label: B
choices.text: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, whereas the left branches directly off the aortic arch

choices.label: C
choices.text: The right arises from the subclavian and the left from the pulmonary trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: The right arises from the aortic arch and the left from the vertebral artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both arise from the brachiocephalic trunk but on opposite sides

explanation.summary: The aortic arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian. The brachiocephalic trunk then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian, so only the right common carotid is a second-order branch.
explanation.whyCorrect: The aortic arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian. The brachiocephalic trunk then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian, so only the right common carotid is a second-order branch.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only the coronary arteries arise from the ascending aorta; the carotids come from the arch.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither carotid arises from the subclavian or pulmonary trunk; the pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the anatomy, and the vertebral artery is a branch of the subclavian, not a source of the carotid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is only one brachiocephalic trunk, on the right; the left common carotid arises directly from the arch.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This figure shows the arterial anastomoses of the nasal septum, including the anterior plexus outlined at the front. What common clinical event is this anterior region most associated with?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the sense of smell

explanation.summary: The anterior septal anastomosis (Kiesselbach plexus) is a superficial convergence of several arteries and is the site of roughly 90% of nosebleeds. The posterior Woodruff plexus accounts for less common but heavier posterior bleeds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anterior septal anastomosis (Kiesselbach plexus) is a superficial convergence of several arteries and is the site of roughly 90% of nosebleeds. The posterior Woodruff plexus accounts for less common but heavier posterior bleeds.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Recurrent sinus infections relate to impaired sinus drainage through the ostia, not the anterior septal vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Referred ear pain travels via shared nerves such as CN V, IX, and X, not via a vascular plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Obstructive sleep apnea involves collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep, not septal vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of smell relates to the olfactory epithelium in the nasal roof, not the anterior septal plexus.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: The paranasal sinuses are shown draining into the nasal cavity. Which of these sinuses is the largest and most frequently involved in sinusitis?

explanation.summary: The maxillary sinuses are the largest paranasal sinuses. Because their ostium sits high on the medial wall, gravity-dependent drainage is poor, making them the most commonly infected sinus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The maxillary sinuses are the largest paranasal sinuses. Because their ostium sits high on the medial wall, gravity-dependent drainage is poor, making them the most commonly infected sinus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ethmoid air cells are multiple small cells; ethmoid sinusitis is prominent in children but they are not the largest sinus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mastoid air cells lie in the temporal bone and connect to the middle ear, not the nasal cavity, so they are not a paranasal sinus.

questions.stem: On this normal PA chest radiograph, why do the lung fields appear dark (radiolucent) compared with the central heart shadow?

choices.text: Bone in the lung fields scatters the beam away from the detector

choices.text: The lungs contain dense muscle that blocks the X-ray beam

questions.stem: The airways from the trachea through the terminal bronchioles are grouped as the 'conducting zone.' What physiological property defines this zone?

choices.text: It is the primary site of oxygen–carbon dioxide exchange

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is lined entirely by gas-exchanging alveoli

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: It actively secretes surfactant to reduce surface tension

choices.label: E

explanation.summary: The conducting zone (trachea to terminal bronchioles) warms, humidifies, and channels air but has no alveoli, so it constitutes anatomic dead space. Gas exchange begins only in the respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and sacs).
explanation.whyCorrect: The conducting zone (trachea to terminal bronchioles) warms, humidifies, and channels air but has no alveoli, so it constitutes anatomic dead space. Gas exchange begins only in the respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and sacs).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gas exchange occurs in the respiratory zone, which begins at the respiratory bronchioles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The conducting zone has no alveoli; alveoli begin in the respiratory zone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Capillaries first exchange with air in the alveolar walls of the respiratory zone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surfactant is secreted by type II pneumocytes in the alveoli, not by conducting airways.

explanation.summary: On a well-inspired PA chest film, roughly 9-10 posterior ribs (or 5-6 anterior ribs) should be visible above the diaphragm. Fewer ribs suggests a poor inspiratory effort, which can mimic or obscure pathology such as basal atelectasis or increased lung markings.
explanation.whyCorrect: On a well-inspired PA chest film, roughly 9-10 posterior ribs (or 5-6 anterior ribs) should be visible above the diaphragm. Fewer ribs suggests a poor inspiratory effort, which can mimic or obscure pathology such as basal atelectasis or increased lung markings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rotation is judged by the symmetry of the medial clavicle ends around the spinous processes, not by counting ribs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rib fractures are identified by examining cortical breaks along each rib, not by counting ribs above the diaphragm.

questions.stem: This figure separates the muscles of inspiration from the muscles of expiration. During QUIET (resting) breathing, expiration is accomplished mainly by which mechanism?

explanation.whyCorrect: Quiet expiration is passive: the inspiratory muscles relax and the stored elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall drives air out. The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals shown here are recruited only for active, forced expiration such as coughing or exercise.

whyWrongByChoice.C: Internal intercostal contraction is used only in forced expiration, not quiet breathing.

questions.stem: This figure contrasts the chest and diaphragm during breathing in versus breathing out. During inspiration, how does diaphragm contraction change intrathoracic pressure and drive airflow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It relaxes and ascends, pulling air into the lungs

choices.label: B
choices.text: It domes upward, decreasing thoracic volume and pushing air in

choices.label: C
choices.text: It flattens and descends, lowering intrapleural/alveolar pressure so air flows in

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raises alveolar pressure above atmospheric, drawing air in

choices.label: E
choices.text: It has no effect on volume; only the ribs move air

explanation.summary: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens and moves down, enlarging the thoracic cavity. By Boyle's law the increased volume lowers intrapleural and alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in. During quiet expiration the diaphragm relaxes and ascends, the lungs recoil, and air passively flows out.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens and moves down, enlarging the thoracic cavity. By Boyle's law the increased volume lowers intrapleural and alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in. During quiet expiration the diaphragm relaxes and ascends, the lungs recoil, and air passively flows out.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Relaxation and ascent of the diaphragm occur during expiration and push air out.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doming upward decreases thoracic volume, which raises pressure and expels air rather than drawing it in.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Air flows in only when alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric, not above it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The diaphragm is the main muscle changing thoracic volume, accounting for most of quiet inspiration.
